analysis.one_liner: Repeals the medical device excise tax, paid for by ending tax breaks for major oil companies.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 6 cosponsors, died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Affordable Care Act imposed a 2.3% excise tax on the sale of medical devices. This bill would have repealed that tax for device makers and paid for it by closing three tax breaks available only to the largest oil companies: a domestic production deduction, last-in-first-out (LIFO) accounting, and certain foreign tax credits. The oil provisions were designed to offset the lost revenue, so the swap was roughly revenue-neutral on paper.
analysis.who_benefits: Medical device manufacturers gain directly, since they would no longer pay the 2.3% excise tax on their sales. Patients and hospitals could benefit indirectly if any of the savings were passed through in device prices, though that pass-through is not guaranteed. The largest integrated oil companies lose, since the bill would deny them the tax deductions and credits it uses to pay for the repeal.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2.3% excise tax on medical device sales, effective for sales after enactment, removing a tax the device industry said raised costs and hurt hiring.
Covers the cost by denying major integrated oil companies the domestic production tax deduction for oil and gas income, barring them from LIFO accounting, and limiting their foreign tax credits.

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies — firms with at least 500,000 barrels of daily worldwide production and over $1 billion in gross receipts — would bear the cost of the repeal, losing the deductions and credits that fund it.

drawbacks.text: The direct beneficiary is a concentrated industry: the repeal puts billions of dollars a year back in the hands of device makers, with no guarantee patients see lower prices.
Oil companies and their allies argued that closing these deductions and accounting methods would raise their costs of domestic production, which critics said could put upward pressure on fuel prices.
Repealing the device tax removes a revenue stream that fell on an industry whose sales grew because the same law expanded health coverage to millions of new customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward trade between two industries: a tax cut for device makers, paid for by closing oil company tax breaks, roughly balancing out fiscally. Ordinary people stand to gain only indirectly, through possible device price effects, while the clearest gainers are the device manufacturers themselves. It is a modest, revenue-neutral bill rather than a large transfer to the public or from it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the Congress ended in January 2015 with the bill dead.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Maffei introduced the bill on March 20, 2013, joined by Rep. Jared Polis.
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day and received no further action.
It drew 6 Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 113th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies kept their tax deductions and credits, and the medical device industry kept paying the 2.3% excise tax it had sought to repeal — both concentrated interests stayed where they were, and the Treasury kept the status quo revenue. (Note: the device tax was separately suspended and later repealed in later Congresses, outside this bill.)

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies kept their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Dan Maffei
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the medical device excise tax with oil company tax breaks as the offset.

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill, letting it die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored exclusively by Democrats (the sponsor plus 6 Democratic cosponsors), and it died in a Republican-controlled committee without any recorded votes, so no roll-call pattern exists to measure the split.

industries.note: The bill would repeal the 2.3% excise tax on their sales, a direct and permanent gain. The industry argued the tax raised device costs and cost jobs; whether patients actually share in the savings depends on pricing decisions the bill cannot control.

The bill would strip them of the domestic production deduction, LIFO accounting, and certain foreign tax credits, making them the pay-for for the device tax repeal. Their tax advantages cost the Treasury revenue that general taxpayers otherwise make up.
